key_facts: **Melasma** is acquired, symmetrical brown patches on the face (cheeks, forehead, upper lip, chin), driven by **UV, visible light and hormones**.
Commonest in women with Fitzpatrick III–V skin; triggered by pregnancy ('mask of pregnancy') and the combined pill.
Wood's light or dermoscopy suggests epidermal versus dermal pigment; dermal pigment responds poorly.
Foundation: daily **tinted** broad-spectrum SPF 30–50 (iron oxides block visible light); azelaic acid 15–20%; avoid unregulated bleaching creams.
Specialist: triple-combination creams, tranexamic acid, peels; relapse is common. Consider drug-induced pigmentation and exogenous ochronosis.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Melasma** is an acquired disorder of facial hyperpigmentation — symmetrical brown to grey-brown patches on sun-exposed face. It is commoner in women of reproductive age and in darker skin phototypes, but men are affected too.

This page also covers **exogenous ochronosis** (hydroquinone-related blue-black pigment) and a brief note on **drug photosensitivity/pigmentation**, which sit in the same facial-melanosis teaching week.

sub: About 90% are women; onset in the 20s–40s; common in Latin American, East and South Asian, Middle Eastern and African skin.

ul: Genetic predisposition plus **UV and visible light**, heat, pregnancy and hormonal contraception, thyroid disease, and cosmetics/irritation.
Melanocytes overproduce melanin; pigment may sit in epidermis, dermis, or both (Wood’s lamp / clinical pattern).
**Exogenous ochronosis:** prolonged topical hydroquinone (often unregulated bleaching creams) → dermal ochre pigment; can be permanent.
**Drug photosensitivity:** tetracyclines, thiazides, amiodarone, NSAIDs, quinolones, sulfonylureas and others cause photo-distributed eruptions or slate pigment.
Sun (UVA, UVB and **visible light**), oestrogen and progesterone, heat, genetics; possibly thyroid disease.
Irritant cosmetics, phototoxic products.
**"SPF 50 alone is enough"**: ordinary sunscreens do not block visible light; use a tinted one.
**"Stronger bleach works faster"**: high-strength hydroquinone or mercury/steroid creams cause ochronosis and harm.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: In melasma, **overactive melanocytes** and a damaged dermis keep producing pigment.

mech.t: UV and visible light, heat and hormones stimulate melanocytes and keratinocytes.
Melanocytes enlarge and transfer more melanin to keratinocytes (epidermal melasma).
mech.caption: Melasma: light and hormones stimulate enlarged melanocytes to pass extra pigment into the epidermis; some pigment drops into dermal melanophages.

mech.t: Pigment falls into the dermis and is taken up by melanophages; this dermal component is hard to treat.
Solar elastosis, increased blood vessels and a damaged basement membrane keep stimulating melanocytes, explaining relapse.

histo: Increased epidermal melanin, prominent melanocytes, dermal melanophages, solar elastosis and vessels. Biopsy rarely needed.

ul: Centro-facial, malar or mandibular patterns; upper lip common.
Usually asymptomatic; psychological impact can be high.
Exogenous ochronosis: speckled blue-black “caviar” papules on treated sites.
Drug photo-eruptions: sharp cut-off at clothing, sparing under chin and upper eyelids.

blocks.title: Skin of colour
blocks.text: Melasma is commoner and often mixed epidermal–dermal. Judge severity on colour contrast and area, not redness.

sub: Often fades after delivery; azelaic acid is the safer option; avoid retinoids and hydroquinone.

blocks.title: Hydroquinone caution
blocks.text: Long-term or high-strength HQ (especially from unregulated creams) risks exogenous ochronosis. Prefer time-limited specialist courses only.

refer.t: Blue-black speckled pigment after bleaching creams → stop HQ, refer.
Diagnostic doubt with lichenoid or contact pigment → dermatology (biopsy ± patch testing).
Sudden photo-distributed pigment with systemic drug — review the culprit with the original prescriber.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Blue-black speckled pigment after bleaching creams → stop HQ, refer.
Diagnostic doubt with lichenoid or contact pigment → dermatology (biopsy ± patch testing).
Sudden photo-distributed pigment with systemic drug — review the culprit with the original prescriber.
Psychological impact; post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation from irritating treatments; exogenous ochronosis from hydroquinone.
Chronic and relapsing, worse in summer; strict photoprotection is lifelong.

pearls: The single most important advice is **strict photoprotection including visible light** (tinted sunscreen), not another cream.
Melasma in pregnancy: sunscreen, camouflage and azelaic acid; defer stronger agents.
Ask specifically about imported “fairness” creams — they may hide steroids, mercury or HQ.
Set expectations: months of improvement, and relapse is common without ongoing sun protection.

quiz.q: When should you think of Melasma & facial melanosis?
quiz.a: Symmetrical brown patches on cheeks, forehead or upper lip in an adult (often after pregnancy or hormonal contraception), worse with sun and heat.
Melanocyte hyperactivity with epidermal ± dermal pigment; UV and visible light, hormones, heat and inflammation drive it.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Daily tinted broad-spectrum SPF 30–50, trigger avoidance, and UK-available lighteners (azelaic acid, retinoid). Refer for specialist combinations.
Exogenous ochronosis from prolonged hydroquinone or illegal bleaching creams — stop HQ and refer; do not escalate lighteners.
